new_statements.second_reader_evidence: File opened: (29-page author PDF of JES 16, 1983; no text layer; scanned in and per-page ocr1983/). Page mapping checked from printed folios: PDF p. 6 = JES p. 133, PDF p. 20 = JES p. 147. Both pages rendered (page render) and read as images. The quoted sentences are there verbatim: p. 133, section 'A Sketch of the Segmental Phonology of Benčnon', third paragraph: 'Benčnon has about forty phonetically different segments and several suprasegmentals (Tone, length, laryngealization, nasalization); but of all these, only tone and 33 segmental phonemes (28 consonants, 5 vowels) are distinctive.'; p. 147, diachronic section on tone 4: 'Another cause for a shift to tone 4 may be the re-interpretat…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Bench is a lexical tone language with five level tones plus one rising toneme; Wedekind's suprasegmental inventory for Bench is tone, length, laryngealization and nasalization, with tone the only distinctive one -- stress is not part of the inventory and no word-stress placement rule is given. The only stress remark is diachronic/contact: final-syllable stress of loanwords (Amharic, Cushitic) is re-interpreted as a high tone (tone 4) on the final syllable. Wedekind 1985b (p. 110) adds the family-level generalisation 'Cushitic languages have phonetic or phonemic stress, Omotic languages, tone'. Lexical items are overwhelmingly monosyllabic (Wedekind 1985: 888, loans are 'the very small set of Bench' polysyllabics'), so a stress rule would be near-vacuous.
new_statements.exceptions: Loanwords (disyllabic) carry a 3-4 rising tone pattern reflecting source-language final stress; no synchronic stress exceptions stated.
new_statements.domain_note: Word/citation-form level; Wedekind's data are elicited citation forms and short phrases from one Addis Ababa speaker (1980-81). No explicit sentence of the form 'Bench has no stress' was found; the reading is inferred from the suprasegmental inventory and the tone-only characterisation.
new_statements.identity_note: Wedekind's 1983 data are from a single Benchnon speaker at Addis Ababa University; Rapold (2006, per Wikipedia summary) treats Benchnon, Shenon and Mernon as mutually intelligible varieties of one language = benc1235. Names in the literature: Bench, Benchnon, Benč non, Gimira, Bench'.

sources.note: Bench described as a five-level (six-toneme) tone language; p. 133 lists the suprasegmentals as tone, length, laryngealization, nasalization (no stress) with only tone distinctive; p. 147: stress of Amharic/Cushitic loans is re-interpreted as a high tone 4, 'conforms with the stress on final syllables in Cushitic and Omotic languages'; the 1983 map (p. 132) puts Benchnon among the '5 Tones' Omotic languages. No word-stress rule for Bench.

sources.note: p. 110: 'Cushitic languages have phonetic or phonemic stress, Omotic languages, tone.' p. 115: 'Gimira-Bench is typologically close to Asian tone languages: it has very few grammatical tone rules, but a high functional load on lexical tone'; lists Gimira/Bench with 5 tone levels (p. 117). Family-level statement, not Bench-specific stress rule.
Tertiary; states six phonemic tones (five level + rising 23), nothing on stress; supplied the working URLs for the Wedekind PDFs and the Leiden summary.
